newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to rule on Anglo/Lonrho before May 5.
newsitem.headline: EU to rule on Anglo/Lonrho before May 5.

text.p: The European Commission declined to comment on Wednesday on a report that European Union investigators had recommended banning Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd from keeping a 28 percent stake in Lonrho Plc .

The Wall Street Journal reported that Commission competition officials had moved to deny regulatory approval of the acquisition by the South African mining giant, a decision that had been backed by an advisory committee of national officials.
A spokesman for Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said he had no comment on the report, saying the EU executive would decide on the issue by May 5 at the latest.
The Wall Street Journal said the Commission was expected to follow the preliminary rulings.
An EU source confirmed that the advisory committee had met but declined to disclose the outcome of the meeting.
Saying there was nothing one could add to the article, the source added: "When the Commission starts a detailed (competition) probe it is because the deal can raise serious competition problems."

Anglo American increased its Lonrho shareholding to 28.4 percent from 10 percent in November, despite Van Miert's warnings that it should not try to take control of Lonrho's platinum interests based in South Africa.

Van Miert's position, which he has stated publicly, is that Anglo cannot keep its 28-percent stake unless it gives up control of Lonrho's platinum division. This means that the platinum interests would have to be sold off, something the British conglomerate has seemed to be resisting.
Anglo's stake in Lonrho effectively puts the platinum market under the control of the two companies and Gencor Ltd of South Africa.
Together they control 63 percent of the world's output and 90 percent of the world's reserves. The EU's merger regulation bans creation or strengthening of a dominant position.
In December, the EU executive opened an in-depth investigation into Anglo's stake in the British-based conglomerate.

It said at the time it feared Anglo's control of Lonrho could lead to a dominant position in the platinum and rhodium markets, two precious metals used in the manufacture of car catalytic converters to reduce gas emissions.
Industry sources and lawyers have said there are only two things Anglo could do: convince Lonrho to sell its platinum interests or reduce its shareholding.
In April last year, the Commission blocked the merger of the platinum interests of Lonrho and Gencor because the market would be dominated by a duopoly.
